entries.test: Compare the cited AGI-arrival arguments with historical definitions to determine whether they substitute benchmark performance for real-world flexibility.
entries.note: The normalization changes historical centrality into an unqualified claim about what AGI is.

entries.test: Public evaluations of systems available at publication can establish whether they meet the robustness, generalization, and autonomy criteria specified in the post.
entries.note: The surrounding text gives the headline a substantive reading and specifies the standards being invoked.

entries.test: Public evaluations can show whether impressive task performance coexists with failures of the broader generalization and autonomy criteria specified in the post.
entries.note: This concerns the sufficiency of task performance as evidence under the stated criteria.
The distinction between statistical approximation and intelligence itself lacks a shared empirical dividing line.

entries.test: Compare Chen et al.'s definitions and argument with historical AGI definitions to determine whether their conclusion depends on changed criteria.
entries.note: The claim concerns a publicly available argument and historical definitions.

entries.test: Compare public evaluations of contemporary systems with the robustness, generalization, and failure-resistance criteria in Hendrycks et al. (2025).
entries.note: Marcus endorses the shortfall assessment in the coauthored text.

entries.test: Compare published AGI definitions and public system evaluations with the original standards identified in the post.
entries.note: “We see no evidence” becomes the stronger “there is no evidence”; attempted weakening also becomes accomplished weakening.
The full claim judges how intelligence should be evaluated. Its historical comparison is separately checkable.

entries.test: Public comparisons of benchmark scores and performance under novel environments can establish the limits of benchmarks as indicators of the stated AGI capabilities.
entries.note: The surrounding discussion supplies a plain reading of “limited”: benchmark success can coexist with failures of generalization.

entries.test: Published benchmark audits and reproducible gaming demonstrations can establish how commonly simple shortcuts inflate AI benchmark scores.
entries.note: “Often” and “easily” permit empirical assessment despite lacking numerical thresholds.

entries.test: Public training disclosures and benchmark-contamination studies over time can establish whether direct benchmark training became more frequent as financial stakes increased.
entries.note: The source states concurrent trends; “have led” adds a definite causal commitment.

entries.test: Controlled public studies comparing benchmark-focused training with alternative training can measure its effect on performance under modest distribution shifts.
entries.note: The source explicitly links optimization for benchmarks to degraded performance elsewhere.

entries.test: Representative occupational-task evaluations of systems available at publication can measure the fraction of tasks they perform reliably.
entries.note: Whether the cited studies actually support this assertion is a factual question, not a checkability barrier.

entries.test: The cited report and representative firm surveys can establish the share reporting economically meaningful returns from AI deployment.
entries.note: The normalization drops “evidence suggests.” The claim has a measurable factual core despite its interpretive closing clause.

entries.test: Public real-world evaluations can establish whether contemporary systems consistently demonstrate flexibility, cross-domain generalization, and reliability under the post's criteria.
entries.note: “Evidence suggests” characterizes existing evidence here, rather than assigning a chance to a future outcome.

entries.test: Public studies can test whether human-like outputs alone predict independently measured judgment, error correction, or generalization capabilities.
entries.note: “No insight” is a strong claim that evidence of predictive information could challenge.

entries.test: The methods and results of Loru et al. (2025) can establish model confidence when news-source inputs explicitly signal uncertainty.
entries.note: The normalization omits “tended to” and broadens the description beyond the particular comparison.

entries.test: Public training documentation and controlled comparisons in the named domains can test whether model judgments track linguistic plausibility while human judgments respond to reasons, stakes, and responsibility.
entries.note: The normalization drops the specified domains and makes the contrast an unrestricted claim about language models.

entries.test: Public evaluations of contemporary systems can establish limitations in robustness across environments, generalization under novelty, and autonomous goal-directed behavior.
entries.note: The source explicitly identifies what “original AGI standards” means.

entries.test: Public autonomous-task evaluations can measure goal persistence, long-horizon reasoning performance, and required human assistance in contemporary LLMs.
entries.note: “Today's” refers to the publication date.

entries.test: Public proof records and evaluations of the same systems can establish whether isolated mathematical successes demonstrate the broader AGI capabilities specified in the post.
entries.note: In context, “do not alter this assessment” denies that these proofs establish the stated general capabilities.

entries.test: Public evaluations varying prompts and deployment conditions can measure brittleness and inconsistency in reliability, resistance to systematic failure, and cross-domain transfer.
entries.note: The normalization omits “on these dimensions,” broadening the scope beyond the preceding specified capabilities.

entries.test: Public evaluations of systems available at publication can establish whether they exhibit flexible, self-directed competence under the original AGI criteria described in the post.
entries.note: The normalization drops the restriction to the original AGI concept and omits the claims of power and increasing usefulness.
“Risks” asserts a possible consequence, not a firm outcome.
Calling the conflation a strategic misjudgment expresses an evaluative conclusion, rather than empty rhetoric.
